utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we speaking about the group of houses here below?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Marked number 1 --

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The well, the cowshed, anywhere. Did you go anywhere else in that compound, apart from the oda? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karpuzi, my final question is this: The evidence this Tribunal has heard over the last weeks and months may lead it to conclude that while you were sitting listening to Qerqizi singing, there were people chained up, being tortured and possibly even murdered in that compound through the months of April, May, June and July. Now, bearing that in mind, did you see or hear anything while you were there that suggested that such a thing might be going on under your nose?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true, absolutely not. I've told this to the investigator because he asked me the same thing, but this is strange. I have neither seen nor heard about such a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Topolski. Mr. Guy-Smith, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It is, and I will be but a moment because I need to move. Cross-examined by Mr. Guy-Smith:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karpuzi.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I represent Haradin Bala. I would -- I'd like to start with an understanding of something that you just said to Mr. Topolski regarding where people stayed. Because you indicated that everybody did not stay together because you were worried or concerned about shelling coming from the Serbs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were to take a look once again at one of the maps from an aerial view, which I know is difficult, would you be able by looking at that map to point out for the Trial Chamber the various places where people stayed?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karpuzi be supplied with I believe it's 128? I could be incorrect about that -- no, I'm sorry, the aerial map. DM3. I'm not going to have any of your stickers moved, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Taking a look at DM3, which is an aerial view of the area, are you able to recognise any of the houses where the soldiers stayed at night?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see that you're using a pointer there, and if we have another -- I think we actually do because I got a fresh copy of it from the Prosecution. I'm giving you a choice of either stickers or a Bic pen. The pen in your hand may well be -- if you could put on the map those places and mark them sequentially 1, 2, 3, 4, the places where soldiers stayed at night in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I start?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I ask you to pause, Mr. Guy-Smith, I'm sorry. We need to turn off the ELMO and adjust and restart it again to try and improve the image.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely. I don't know if that's any better. I don't find it to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It was an attempt to improve --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Nothing can be done further to improve it at the moment. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to use -- go back to the map now if you could. And if you could mark with a number 1 one of the places where soldiers stayed, if you can recognise it from the aerial map that you have there in front of you.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I mark all the houses or just one of them? Because it's a large number of houses that we've been to during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, indeed, mark as many of the houses as you can, sir, all of them. That would be excellent. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It might be easier to put a ring around it -- a circle around it, each house.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You seem to be marking quite a number of places, Mr. Karpuzi.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm marking those places where we have been during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there more to mark?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that I've marked a few more because I've never seen an aerial map before. I have never analysed it, so there might be a smaller mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Let me ask you this: While you have that map in front of you looking at it from an aerial position - and I understand you've never had that view before - as you look at that map, does that map contain all of the area of Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just the part where we participated in combat, part of the defence line, because Lapusnik is much bigger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... as you sit here today were soldiers in other parts of Lapusnik where they spent the evening?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One part of the soldiers were usually working on shifts on the defence line. And at night they would sleep in different odas and different houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before we leave the issue of the houses that you've marked, is it possible that there are a few less houses than you actually stayed in as well as a few more as you look at the map? So what I'm trying to get at just so I'm clear: Have you marked to your satisfaction all of the houses or could more houses have been marked?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are other houses that have not been marked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with regard to the people who were fighting at Lapusnik, the people who were at the points at Lapusnik during the time that you were there, I want to mention some names to you and see whether or not these names you remember as people who were fighting either alongside you or people who you saw. Okay? Neseri - and my pronunciations may be incorrect and if they are I apologise. Nasufi?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nasufi, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Drini?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an Agim, a soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Agim's pseudonym was?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. No objection, I just don't think the translation caught the question because Mr. Guy-Smith was asking the question while the interpreters were still translating the answer to the previous question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Agim's pseudonym was?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Graniti?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Minatori?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Skifter?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Uka?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Genci?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Motori?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cubi?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fati?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Luzhi?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rambo?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you sit here right now, do you recall any of the other names of the men or women that you fought with during this time?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to move on another issue. When you were discussing record-keeping, are the names that I've mentioned to you here, the ones that you remembered, are those some of the people that you kept records of?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you sit here today, are all of those people still alive or are some of those people fallen in the defence of your country?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those that you mentioned, Motori, Agimi, Minatori, these are alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The others, those pieces of paper moved to the other shelf in the oda of Gzim?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not that we moved them to another shelf, but the details of these names -- so these are the names that I kept records about, their date of birth, their year of birth, their economic status, and details about the weapon they possessed. It's about these persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we give Mr. Karpuzi I believe it's 135. Plaintiff's [sic] 135.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as I understand your testimony, this is a gathering of men to celebrate the anniversary of Ymer Alushani's death. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And looking at -- looking at Plaintiff's 135, in the very back of the photo there I believe is a headstone with what seems to me to be a likeness, the face, of this commander. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the picture of Voglushi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this particular monument was a monument that was put up after the war. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I was to mention the year 2002 to you, would that refresh your recollection with regard to when this photograph was taken? It may, it may not.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but approximately it was taken in 2002. I don't know exactly, but I know that the memorial was erected quite a long time after the war ended. Here it is as well written when this memorial was built and the picture shows us there during the anniversary of Ymer Alushani's fall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to spend a moment with you discussing your statement, and I know you've spent a lot of time with this and I'm not going to dwell on it. But I would just like to get some clarification if we possibly could as to what occurred. Your first statement was given on the 19th and 21st of July, 2003. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When that statement was being taken, and we've had some description of what occurred, to your knowledge was that statement tape-recorded?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean by the investigator?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no. Legally it wasn't and illegally everything can happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not as you recall whether or not anybody was running a video camera or a camera of the time when you were speaking with the gentleman you've called Ole?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no. I couldn't see it. It wasn't visible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I understand the statement went over a two-day period. I'd like to just deal with the first day the statement was being taken. And during that period of time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Guy-Smith. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just want to put on the record the statement was not tape-recorded or videotaped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the first day when the statement was being taken, you were there; Ole was there, who is an investigator from the ICTY; and somebody was there who is a translator also. Right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did your conversation with Mr. Lehtinen, which is his last name, the investigator, was your conversation to him similar to what's been happening here in court, which is he would ask you a question, you would give him an answer, he would ask you another question? Or were you having a conversation with this man?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Every answer of mine followed his question. So the questions came first and then I answered. I explained this to the gentleman, in fact Mr. Nicholls. I told him on Sunday that this was a misunderstanding between Ole and myself during the conversation. I also added that in the end on the 21st I was so stressed that I told him, Take these papers and go and I will not sign them. And the reason for that was that I would say something differently and I had to ask the interpreter, Hey, interpreter, are you telling the investigator this or is he saying something else? And then Ole said, All right, all right. And then he had to remove those parts that I didn't say. And then I asked again the interpreter, Sir, did I say this? And then Ole reviewed those parts where I saw bigger mistakes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you sit here today, can you tell us how many times you had to get Ole to remove things from your statement that you didn't say?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. On the first day he just took notes. I didn't know what he was writing, but he was just writing. He would ask the question, then I would answer; he would again ask a question, and I would again answer. It lasted for some four hours, I'm not quite sure; between three and four hours. Then when they brought the statement before me to sign it, I asked for an Albanian copy. I wanted to have an Albanian copy of what I said. And he said to me that according to the Tribunal it's not allowed to give you a copy. We will read you the statement in Albanian and then you decide for yourself whether you will sign it or not. Then the interpreter read back the statement to me in Albanian. I would tell my remarks, and then Ole would say to me, Well, this is not that important. And to me, maybe I didn't know what the weight of that word was. So this is how it basically happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say that he would indicate to you that something you were trying to correct in your statement was not that important. Do you know if he was making notes with regard to what you said was not correct in your statement? Did he show you at any point in time what he was doing on that computer?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he keep -- as you sit here if you remember, did he keep your corrections, what you said needed to be corrected, on the computer?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what happened. Prior to my signing the statement I objected. And each time he met me, I told him, Ole, this is not right. Even in the presence of Mr. Nicholls, who -- together with two other colleagues, I was obliged to explain to them that some things need to be corrected, in addition to that even on Sunday when I was here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before you met with Mr. Nicholls on Sunday, you met with Mr. Nicholls once before, as I understand your testimony. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was a meeting that you had with Mr. Nicholls, I believe, back home. It wasn't here in The Hague, was it?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it was back home, yes. He was with Ole. I took -- I mean, I asked them to come in. I don't remember if they drank something or not, but I know that it was Mr. Nicholls and his colleague wearing glasses. They introduced themselves to me by their true names and they told me that they are the Prosecutor's counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that meeting with Mr. Nicholls, did you discuss any of your experiences in the spring and summer, fall and winter of 1998 or your experiences as a soldier during this war?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't -- Mr. Nicholls didn't ask me at all about such experiences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss with Mr. Nicholls the previous statement that you had made?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls -- I didn't address Mr. Nicholls, I addressed the investigator, Ole, asking him to see that in the statement, since I didn't know English, it was not translated in English -- in Albanian, it was only a page in English. It was in English. I kindly asked them to correct some mistakes that I thought were in certain places, and they told me, We can do that when we come to The Hague. And this is what we did on Sunday with Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've forgotten. When did you meet with Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some time, one week before the trial started here I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when you met with him in October, when you met with him at your home, when was that?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date, but it was before the trial started here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how long after you met with Mr. Lehtinen in 2003 that you met with Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a considerable time lapse I think. I don't remember when that was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you met with Mr. Nicholls, did you identify your specific concerns about what could be incorrect in your statement? Did you say to Mr. Nicholls something along the lines of, Listen, I have some concerns about some of the things that were taken down and I want them to be corrected?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know the importance. I didn't know what position he had. That's why I often addressed Ole, telling him that this is wrong, this is wrong, this is wrong. But Ole answered me, telling me that, We will correct them; they don't matter much. When you come there, when you give your testimony, we will see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were telling Ole about your concerns, as you sit here today do you remember whether Ole was taking notes about what your concerns were? Was he writing down what were your problems?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this. I don't remember this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It actually is an excellent time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karpuzi, I'd like to return for a moment to the Lapusnik area and ask you a couple of questions with regard to those matters. Specifically: During the evening when you were sleeping, did you have people guarding or watching the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't get interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then let me try again and see whether or not it's coming to you.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you that during the time that you were sleeping, did you have an individual who was guarding you? Was somebody designated as a guard for the sleeping soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that individual change or was it always the same individual, if you remember, with regard to your unit?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was changed every four hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were in Lapusnik, were you able to go anywhere you chose to go in the compound which was called -- has been called the Gzim compound?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've mentioned that you would on occasion go across the street and go into the oda where you would sing. And in that particular compound, were you free to go wherever you wished to go?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with regard to other areas, other homes in Lapusnik, would it be fair to say that this was one large community where each of you were living with each other, helping each other, soldier or civilian, and there was free access to all the homes?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have one more question to ask you, and that revolves around somebody who Mr. Topolski asked you about. So perhaps once again we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: If it pleases Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Khan:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karpuzi, I represent Mr. Fatmir Limaj. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I know this has been a long three days for you. You'll be pleased to hear that I hope I will not be too long and it may be the case, subject to the Prosecution and the leave of the Court, that we can finish with your testimony today. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to your education, I think you said yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And Your Honours, it's at page 5 -- sorry, two days ago at page 5 of the LiveNote transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that after primary school you had only two years of high school. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you could not go on with your education because of the Serb repression and the difficulties that Kosovar Albanians were encountering. Those problems touched you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So much so that I think that you told my learned friend Mr. Nicholls who was asking you questions that in a five-year period you had been arrested also by the Serbs about five times. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karpuzi, it may seem like an awfully silly question, but perhaps it will help Their Honours understand the issues which they have decide, so please bear with me. Am I right if I -- in my understanding that at school you never went through a text, for example, Shakespeare, line by line and word by word. Would that be fair or not?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be fair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the first time that you went through such an exercise was in fact these last two days with Mr. Nicholls. That's the first time you've Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. gone through a document, a text, in such detail word by word, line by line. Would that be a fair comment or would it be unfair?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a fair comment. This is how it happened. You were present yourself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you find that process? Did you find it easy or difficult to perform that task line by line, word by word with Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a hard process for me because I have never been subjected to such situations. I have often emphasised that many things are difficult for me to grasp. If it went on for a longer period, I would certainly have said I am incapable of responding to any more questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karpuzi, I am going to talk for a while and ask you questions about a statement that you made to the Prosecution over two days, the 19th and 21st of July, 2003. You're familiar with that statement, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it's a short statement of only seven pages, but you'll understand from the questions you were asked yesterday by my learned friend, Mr. Nicholls, that it's given rise to, let's say, a certain amount of controversy. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some instances there were some controversies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'll try and not repeat -- I'll try my best not to repeat the questions that my learned friend Mr. Guy-Smith asked you. But casting your mind back to the 19th of July, 2003, is it correct that you met Mr. Lehtinen and an interpreter at your home?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you said over the last couple of days that they told you that they'd been sent on behalf of the Prosecutor Carla Del Ponte and they wanted to ask you some questions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you invited these staff members, Mr. Lehtinen and the interpreter, into your home. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Ole Lehtinen asked me if it was possible for them to enter my home and I said yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You wanted to tell a truthful account and help the Tribunal in any way you could. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had great respect, that's why I asked them to come in. I had great respect for the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you still have great respect for the Tribunal. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were your wife -- was your wife and two children at home when the investigator and the interpreter came to your home?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you brought Mr. Lehtinen into your home. Where did you sit?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We sat at the guestroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this interview that you gave lasted some several hours. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve your guests tea or any refreshments on that first visit?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Lehtinen asked you various questions, you answered them, and he tried to put them down on a computer. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Even though he was an investigator, I respected them. I offered them tea and refreshments. You can ask Mr. Lehtinen himself. Out of the respect I had for the Tribunal, I, as I said, offered them tea, refreshments. The first day, the investigator lasted about -- about I think four hours, I can't be accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Going back to my question, Mr. Lehtinen asked you questions and you answered them.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that question-and-answer format was then put into a computer before the next question. Is that right or have I got it wrong?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you've got it right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the structure of the interview was down to Mr. Lehtinen not down to you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if it's a -- and if the statement that resulted from that question-answer format was well-structured, that would be because Mr. Lehtinen had done a very good job. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked questions; I answered them. In most -- in many cases we had misunderstandings, as I said earlier. In several parts I saw things which I had not said. On the 21st, some of them he removed because I insisted that these lines were -- which I didn't say were removed. So I even asked the interpreter, Are you translating it in this way or is he writing what he likes? Because if that is the case, then I will get away -- he can leave with his papers and I won't sign anything. You can ask Mr. Lehtinen about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Let me try again because perhaps I have failed to express myself. I do apologise. The sequence of questions was dictated by Mr. Lehtinen. He decided what to ask and when to ask it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not asked to give a narrative, a general account, first and then you were asked specific questions relating to that account, were you?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- the voice is very loud. Can you please put it down for me. I can't concentrate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karpuzi, it's not your fault it's entirely mine. And for the second time today and perhaps for not the last, I have to apologise to you.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hope I'm not too loud now. Yes. Let me repeat my last question so that the Judges hopefully have an idea of how this statement was generated. You were not asked by Mr. Lehtinen to give an account, a general narrative, you were asked specific questions and gave answers, and that's how the statement was created. That's what you're saying. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll explain. He asked questions of me, but he also allowed me to explain things related to the questions. But he did ask the questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You met Mr. Nicholls again in October of last year, and once again you invited him into your home. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the time when this happened. I didn't invite them [as interpreted]. He came together with Lehtinen and to others, and yes, I of course let them in. I'm sorry that there was nothing on the floor, there was no carpet or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think there Khan may have misspoke when he said "you met Mr. Nicholls again in October." I don't know if he intended to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You met -- along with Mr. Lehtinen, you met Mr. Nicholls sometime last year at your home in Kosova. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think it's important to tell the truth to this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I had not felt it my obligation to tell the truth, I would certainly not be here today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you started giving testimony, you made an affirmation, you promised to tell the truth. Was that important to you or something you think is of little significance?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was interruption in the interpretation. I didn't get your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me try again. Before you started giving testimony three days ago, you made an affirmation, you made an oath. Is that something that you attach importance to or not?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attach great importance to the oath.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have described how you have spoken to the Prosecution on a few occasions, invited them into your house. How do you feel if I tell you that the Prosecution say that you're not willing to tell the truth to this Trial Chamber? How would you feel about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't see the basis. Perhaps it can be elaborated upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, it's completely irrelevant and may refer -- I don't know where he's going with this, but we -- and maybe we should even send the witness out if we're going to pursue this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I simply don't see why. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Relevance, Mr. Khan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the relevance is, in my submission, the witness is quite entitled to be in a position to comment on the importance he gives to evidence before Your Honours on oath in distinction to -- well, as an issue itself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that's enough, and he has done that, has he not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Without qualification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So what is the point of what you're now going to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it goes to the questions that were asked yesterday in relation to the alleged discrepancy between the testimony you heard and the alleged inconsistencies found by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Most assuredly you may deal with those. But what you're now putting is on a different tack, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I -- it must be my fault. I don't see it. In order to proceed, in my submission, in order to understand that the nature of the questions, the witness is entitled to know what the Prosecution view of his testimony, what they consider his testimony to be. And he should be entitled and given an opportunity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, such a very great deal of time was spent yesterday by counsel for the Prosecution identifying differences between the previous statement and the testimony in the course of this trial of the witness, that the witness can have no doubt about that. And I'd have thought you could have no difficulty whatever in directing the witness's attention again to any particular differences that you seek to explore further. And of course, exploring those differences is undoubtedly something that you may properly do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, of course the Prosecution did deal with the issue in quite some considerable detail yesterday. I hope I will not be very long. In my submission, the Prosecution, when the witness is not here, is going to submit as a matter of fact and law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that will do. We're still in the presence of the witness, but I don't think it's necessary for him to go out. Can I suggest, Mr. Khan, that you go on to the substance of any differences and what you want to make from that. You've got an unqualified assurance of the witness's goodwill toward giving an honest account itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I will move on, but in my submission it's quite proper for me to give Your Honours a chance to assess the witness's credibility and his veracity and the importance he gives to his testimony under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have no doubt whatever and could not for a moment question that. But the question you were putting, though, is one that will not assist this Chamber in the matters that are of importance in the case. So if you could move on, Mr. Khan, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that's the case, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked yesterday about an oath ceremony in Lapusnik in June or July 1998. Do you remember being asked many questions by the Prosecution about that?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I know it's difficult to remember matters some time ago, particularly when you told the Trial Chamber that you wanted to forget everything after the war because of all the awful things you had seen. But casting your mind back, is it possible that that oath ceremony took place at the beginning of July rather than in June? Would that help you at all or you can't say?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many times I have repeated that. I'm not certain whether it was end of June or early July. I couldn't specify the time because I don't remember it accurately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've been very clear. My next question, you said yesterday as well that that was the first time you had seen Celiku. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that about 50 people were at this flag-raising ceremony. Did they come from different units or from one unit?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw there 50 or 60 soldiers lined up there, but I didn't know whether they came from different units or from one unit. There were people from different units, but I can't be very accurate about that now. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your experience as a former member of the KLA, was it usual for soldiers of other units to be invited to ceremonial occasions such as oaths or funerals or other events that were being conducted by neighbouring and other units? Was that something that was common or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say that yesterday after the oath and the flag-raising ceremony, the group of 50 broke up. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the group broke up, you had occasion to speak with Celiku, Fatmir Limaj. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have occasion to do that. We were in a group. While we were breaking up -- it was not that I directly spoke with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. This group that Fatmir Limaj spoke to, how many people were in it?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember accurately how many soldiers were there. While we were dispersing from the place, he talked. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again casting your mind back, is it possible that the group of people that Fatmir Limaj spoke to comprised about five or six KLA soldiers? Would that help you recollect what happened or does it provide no assistance at all?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't seem to remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say that when you arrived in Lapusnik on the 8th of May, 1998, that there was no organisation or no presence of KLA troops in Lapusnik at that time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was until soldiers elected Voglushi to be the commander?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've also said a couple of times at least that Isak Musliu, Qerqizi, was later also made a commander in Lapusnik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we seem to have a problem with interpretation. Perhaps it has been solved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Voglushi remained a commander until the end -- well, until he was killed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I think we need to get the answers on the record before we move too far to the questions where it states no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm happy to repeat it. I'm grateful to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karpuzi, there appears to have been a problem with the interpretation, to forgive me with I repeat a question you've already answered. Let's try again. You've already told the Trial Chamber that Isak Musliu, Qerqizi, was made a commander in Lapusnik. You remember saying that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've also said that Voglushi, Ymer Alushani, remained a commander until his death in July 1998. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isak Musliu, you say, was a commander of Celiku 3. Do you know what Ymer Alushani was a commander of, what unit, what was it called?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Celiku 3. As Celiku 3, we knew later. As Celik we knew that we had this name. Then Ymer was elected. We asked him to become our leader. When the number of soldiers increased, Ymer proposed Qerqiz to become one of the leaders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know at that time what Ymer Alushani became a commander of? Do you know or not?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the -- our commander where I was a member too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what it was called?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whom do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After Qerqizi became a commander of Celiku 3, what did Voglushi become a commander of?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Voglushi, too, was a commander. He was our commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that all of these points that you marked on the map in some detail in response to Mr. Topolski's questions, that each of these points had a commander? Would that be correct or not?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were based in Lapusnik as you've said, but do you know who was the commander of Celiku 1?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you heard of a Celiku 1 or Celiku 2?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, what I put to you is that Fatmir Limaj was a commander of Celiku 1. Had you heard about that or not?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As a commander for Fatmir Limaj, I heard that in September, October, or November of 1998, for him as a commander. And before that, I didn't know whether he was a commander and a commander of what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of a time when the KLA in that area started to organise itself and a brigade called the 121 Brigade was formed? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened after the fall of the Lapusnik gorge. I don't know the exact time. I heard about this in October or November. That's when I heard when the 121 Brigade was formed and the smaller units. I don't know now how that -- to put them in the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you answered quite honestly yesterday when you said that you'd heard that Fatmir Limaj became the commander of the 121st, but you didn't directly know it, you didn't directly see it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, you heard that Fatmir Limaj, Celiku, was appointed after the fall of Lapusnik as commander of the 121st. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the fall of the Lapusnik gorge, now -- as I said earlier, I heard it in September, October, or November that he became a commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we go back for a moment to the battle of Lapusnik itself. Would you agree with me that as far as the KLA actions are concerned, that that engagement with the Serbs could hardly be called a coordinated effort? Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact it wasn't coordinated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact there were civilians in the village who were firing at the Serbs. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As well as people from different points that heard the sound of fighting and rushed to join in. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came as an assistance from different points. For example, in one position on the front line you had no idea who it was and from where he came from. You didn't have any time to notice this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps my learned friend has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just think it might be helpful if we put on the record which battle in Lapusnik this is, because there have been several different dates of fighting that the witness has testified about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understood it was the gorge, which I understood to be one in particular. But Mr. Khan no doubt will clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karpuzi, what I was talking about was the first engagement at Lapusnik in May 1998. Was that your understanding or not?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right, in fact, that in that engagement it was the case that KLA members even shot at each other because they didn't know who was doing what where?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that fortuitously, perhaps, because of a stray bullet a petrol tank blew up which caused the Serbs to panic and withdraw? Is that right as far as you know or have I got it wrong?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clear to me. Are we speaking of the occasion when I fired a shell?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Still talking about the first engagement in the 8th of May, 1998.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many bullets flying. The Pinzgauer also was set on fire there on the 9th of May there, at the Lapusnik gorge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say -- you've said earlier today that records were kept for soldiers. This is 16:36:26 of the LiveNote. You said for each soldier there was a piece of paper with the name of the solider, the place of birth and the gun that was issued and these were compiled with respect to each soldier. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when you started keeping those records?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately a month and a half before the fall of the Lapusnik gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the witness can be shown Exhibit P129.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karpuzi, you remember being asked questions about that document by Mr. Nicholls. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One thing I wasn't sure about so I thought it would be useful to get your assistance. Do you say that you saw that particular document in 1998 when you were in Lapusnik? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We kept records about the movement of the Serb army vehicles. It was similar to this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're not saying that you saw that particular document in 1998 in Lapusnik, are you?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in this format. I told the Prosecutor as well that it resembled this one that we kept records about the entrance and departure of the vehicles, how many are withdrawing, how many are coming to that position so that we had an idea about the strength of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'm not asking, Mr. Karpuzi, about the form of the document. Looking at what it says, can you say that you saw that document in Lapusnik containing those sentences whilst you were there in 1998? Can you remember that or you can't?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly this one because this is a copy. It is not possible to have seen this one in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see a document detailing the same facts, the same chronology, the same dates and activities whilst you were in Lapusnik in 1998, or can you not remember?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered this to the Prosecution. I told them I wasn't sure, but approximately it could be this way. Even when I gave my statement, I said that I did not remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know in fact if that was a document actually compiled by the KLA or not. Is that right? Simply you can say it looks similar to the form adopted whilst you were in Lapusnik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I've no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. Mr. Nicholls --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I rise for a brief moment before Mr. Nicholls --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- begins. I have been alerted by the court officer that there is a document that needs to be introduced, and I would ask that it be done so and given the next appropriate number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which document is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is the document which Mr. Karpuzi was kind enough to circle the houses upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be DB2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And now Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a couple topics very quickly. Re-examined by Mr. Nicholls:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived and started fighting in Lapusnik in May 1998 until you were injured on 26th July, 1998, were you always a member of Celiku 3?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now just a couple of questions about the note-taking which you've been asked about. When a soldier came and you - I won't go over the information because you've already explained what information you would record - but how long would it take you on average to put down on paper what you needed for each soldier, about his background, his weapon, that type of thing?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would that be typed or handwritten? Can you explain how you would put that down on paper.

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Typed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about how many of these pieces of paper do you think you put together? How many records did you type up during that month and a half that you were working in the record-keeping?

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 60 or 70 papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: RUZHDI KARPUZI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not precise, but approximately 60 or 70 pieces of paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Karpuzi, you'll be pleased to know that we've come to the end of your evidence. Thank you for your attendance and you're now able to go back to your home. And those assisting you outside will take care of your arrangements. This would seem an opportune time of the day to adjourn. So we will resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
